title: Shepherd of Hermas
subtitle: a Christian of Rome, sold by the man who raised him, sees the Church as an old woman and as a tower, and an angel shepherd offers sinners one more chance to repent
lead: The Shepherd of Hermas is a long Christian book written in Greek in Rome in the second century, or partly a little before. Its writer tells his story in his own voice: the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda in Rome (1:1), and years later, on the road out of the city, heaven began to send him visions. Kirsopp Lake, whose Greek text this site translates, says the book "is in form an apocalypse": a series of revelations made to Hermas "by the Church, who appears in the form of a woman, first old, and afterwards younger; by the shepherd, or angel of repentance; and by the great angel, who is in charge of Christians." Each vision comes with an explanation, and its object, Lake says, "is practical and ethical."

The book has three parts: five Visions (1–25), twelve Mandates or commandments (26–49), and ten Similitudes or parables (50–114). Its great question is what happens to Christians who sin after baptism. Hermas is told that those who have fallen may still repent and be forgiven, but that this repentance is offered once (6:4–5; 31:6). In Lake's summary, "in the Visions the necessity for repentance is enforced, in the Mandates the life required from the penitent is explained, and in the Similitudes the working and theological doctrine of repentance is developed." Its pictures stay with the reader: the Church as an old woman who grows younger as her children repent (8; 18–21), a tower built on water from stones of every kind (10–15; 78–110), a vineyard and a faithful slave (55), twelve mountains and a gate cut in an ancient rock (78–89). With 727 verses it is the longest early Christian writing on this site.

At the edge of the Bible. None of the churches whose Bibles are set out in the canon section below prints the Shepherd in its Bible, and this site translates it as an early Christian writing, never as Scripture. For a time it came very close. About AD 180 Irenaeus quoted words found in its first commandment with "well did the Scripture say," and Eusebius took this to mean that he received the book (Church History 5.8.7), though Irenaeus names neither Hermas nor the Shepherd (Westcott). The fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus copies it with the Epistle of Barnabas after the books of the New Testament (Chapman, 1910; Lake says Barnabas there follows "immediately after the Apocalypse"). Eusebius knew churches that read it in public (Church History 3.3.6). Yet the Muratorian Fragment says it may be read but not read out to the people in church, Tertullian attacked it as the book that "loves adulterers," Eusebius counted it among the spurious books, Athanasius set it outside the canon among books for new believers, and Jerome found it "almost unknown" among Latin Christians. The canon section below sets out each of these.
facts: None of the churches whose New Testament is set out below: it is not in the New Testament listed by the Council of Trent (1546), the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Article VI of the Church of England, the Westminster Confession or the Second London Baptist Confession, nor among the books Reid (1908) says the Coptic and Armenian churches add to the 27. In the early church it stood at the edge of the canon: received by Irenaeus as Eusebius read him (Church History 5.8.7), called "divinely inspired" by Origen in Rufinus's Latin, read publicly in some churches (Eusebius 3.3.6; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 10), copied after the New Testament in Codex Sinaiticus (Chapman), and set outside the canon by the Muratorian Fragment, Eusebius (3.25.4), Athanasius (Festal Letter 39), Jerome (Prologus galeatus) and Rufinus.

Hermas, a Christian of Rome who says that the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda (1:1), with a wife and grown children (6:2–3). The Muratorian Fragment makes him the brother of Pius, bishop of Rome; Origen, in Rufinus's Latin, guessed that he was the Hermas whom Paul greets in Romans 16:14. See "Who was Hermas?" below.

Lake: the Muratorian Fragment's statement that Hermas wrote while his brother Pius was bishop dates the book to "about 148 A.D.", though "many critics" think it was written "at intervals during the twenty or thirty years preceding this date." The Clement named in 8:3 would point to the 90s if he is the Clement of 1 Clement. The Fragment's own date is disputed, and other datings are given below (see "Who was Hermas?").

Rome and its countryside: the Tiber (1:2), the road to Cumae (1:3; 5:1; the Greek has Kōmas, which editors take as Cumae; the Latin has "the city of Ostia"), a farm off the Campanian Way (22:2), a house church with its elders, widows and orphans (8:3). In Similitude 9 the Shepherd carries Hermas to Arcadia in Greece (78:4).
An apocalypse (Lake): visions and their explanations, commandments, and parables, told in the first person.
Greek. The last part survives only in Latin, with a few Greek lines from papyri and a quotation (107:3–114:5).
114 chapters, 727 verses. Chapters 1–114, with the Vision/Mandate/Similitude reference in each chapter title (16:2 is Vision 3.8.2; 31:6 is Mandate 4.3.6; 89:1 is Similitude 9.12.1).

Kirsopp Lake's Greek and Latin, The Apostolic Fathers, vol. 2 (Loeb, 1913), from the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus (to 31:6), the Athos manuscript (A, to 107:2; fifteenth century in Lake, fourteenth in Chapman), papyri, and the Latin, Ethiopic and Coptic versions.
authorship: The writer names himself Hermas (1:4; 2:2). He says that the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda in Rome, and that many years later he came to know her and loved her "as a sister" (1:1). Lake calls the sentence "hardly intelligible" as it stands: "presumably the meaning is that Hermas was born a slave, and that his owner sold him to Rhoda," and that he later "made her acquaintance again"; the alternative is that the verb "merely means 'came to know her properly.'" Chapman notes only that Hermas "is a suitable name for a slave." He had a business that taught him bad habits of mind (7:1), a wife who talked too much (6:3) and children who had sinned and even betrayed their parents (6:2). Through the book he is told to put his household in order (3:1–2; 66:2–3).
The Muratorian Fragment: the brother of Pius

The Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list of New Testament books, says that "Hermas wrote the Shepherd very recently, in our own times, in the city of Rome, while his brother Pius the bishop sat in the chair of the church of the city of Rome" (the site's translation of its Latin, as Westcott prints it, 199). Chapman (1910) adds two more witnesses to the brotherhood, a Roman list of bishops (the Liberian catalogue) and a Latin poem against Marcion, and judges that the three "are probably citing the same papal catalogue"; the Fragment's statement that Hermas wrote during his brother's time as bishop "may similarly be an inference" from finding Hermas named beside Pius in that list. Westcott (1896) took the statement as decisive: "It comes from the place at which the book was written, and dates from the age at which it appeared," the word of "a contemporary Roman writer." Lake follows it. The Fragment's own date is disputed. Its writer calls the Shepherd written "in our own times," and the usual dating is the late second century. Westcott reports that Zahn and Salmon placed it at "the beginning of the third century" (215), and Albert Sundberg (1973) argued that it came from the Greek-speaking East in the fourth century; the later datings have not displaced the second-century one as the consensus (Wikipedia, "Muratorian fragment"). If the later datings are right, "in our own times" is not a contemporary's witness to the book's date.

Paul greets a Hermas among the Christians in Rome (Romans 16:14). Origen thought him the writer: "I think, however, that this Hermas is the writer of that little book called the Shepherd, a writing that seems to me very useful and, as I think, divinely inspired" (Commentary on Romans 10.31, the site's translation of the Latin quoted by Westcott). The commentary survives only in an abridged Latin translation by Rufinus (Prat, 1911), and Westcott warns, of Rufinus's versions of Origen's homilies, that he "was not content to render the simple words of Origen, but sought in several points to bring them into harmony with the current belief" (367). Chapman adds that Origen "repeatedly apologizes, when he has occasion to quote it, on the ground that 'many people despise it'." Eusebius says only that "they say" the book is his (Church History 3.3.6), and Jerome that "they assert" it (Lives of Illustrious Men 10). Westcott calls the identification "nothing more than a conjecture" of Origen's. Chapman lists older writers who held it (Bellarmine, Cave, Lardner and others) and says the Muratorian date had "in the end prevailed amongst scholars." The Orthodox Church in America still commemorates the Apostle Hermas of the Seventy, and says that "according to Tradition" he is the author.

The old woman tells Hermas to send one copy of his little book to Clement, who will send it "to the cities abroad" (8:3). If this is the Clement of 1 Clement, the visions would belong to the 90s, far earlier than Pius. Chapman gives the ways scholars have answered: Hermas may have been much older than his brother; Harnack held that Clement lived into the second century; or, Chapman's own preference, the historical details are a literary device and the writer "wished to be thought to belong to the preceding generation." Lake, in his introduction to 1 Clement, says the line "certainly points to a Clement in Rome exercising the same functions as the writer of I. Clement," but that Hermas is probably somewhat later and the reference "may be merely a literary device based on knowledge of the earlier book."

Lake reports that "many critics" see "traces ... of varying dates in the three divisions of the book." Chapman (1910) names theories of two writers (De Champagny), three (Hilgenfeld), a Christian reworking of a Jewish book (Spitta), and a later addition of Visions 1–4 (Haussleiter), and judges that the "unity of style and matter" answers them; Harnack, in Chapman's account, dated the core of Vision 2 before 110 and the finished book between 135 and 145. The book itself says it was written down in stages (8:2; 25:5–7; 78:1).

audience.to: The Christians of Rome, in the second century or a little before (the date is disputed: see "Date" above): house churches led by elders, with widows and orphans in their care. The old woman tells Hermas to make two copies of his book, one for Clement to send "to the cities abroad" and one for Grapte, who will teach the widows and orphans, while Hermas himself is to read it "in this city" with the elders who lead the church (8:3). He is to warn a man named Maximus (7:4), speak to the leaders of the church (6:6; 17:7), and set right his own household (3:1–2; 6:2–3; 66). The visions are told to "brothers" (8:1), and the closing chapters send the book out to all who will listen (25:5–7; 111–114). The Muratorian Fragment, whose writer says the book was written "very recently, in our own times," allows it to be read but not read out to the people in church.
audience.why: To call a church that had grown comfortable back to repentance while there was still time. Some of its members had denied the Lord (6:8; 7:4; 14:5; 74:4), some had been brought before the authorities (105:4), some were tangled in business and wealth (14:5–6; 97), some were double-minded, and many believed, Lake says, that a Christian who sinned after baptism "could not again obtain forgiveness." Hermas brings word that God has opened one more door: those who have fallen may repent, once, and be received (6:4–5; 29–31), but the time is short (6:5; 113–114). Knowing this audience changes how the book reads. Its long lists of stones and sticks are not a general allegory of human nature but a roll call of real kinds of Roman Christians, and its one repentance is a pastoral offer to a particular church, which later churches argued over (see the chapter page of 31).
views: Lake and Chapman both take the book as a Roman work, and the details bear it out: the Tiber (1:2), the road to Cumae (1:3), the Campanian Way (22:2), and the instruction to read it "in this city" with its elders (8:3). Chapman sees in 8:3 the church of Rome at work: the elders who lead, Grapte with the widows, and Clement who writes to other churches.

The great suffering that is coming (6:7; 24:6), those who had denied the Lord (6:8; 7:4; 14:5) and those brought before the authorities who did not deny him (105:4) point, on this page's reading, to persecution, past and expected. Westcott thought the book's tone and its view of discipline and church order fit the age of Montanism, the later second century, better than the apostolic age.

The book was meant to travel (8:3), and it did: Clement of Alexandria quotes it often, Origen, in Rufinus's Latin, called it "divinely inspired," Eusebius says churches read it in public (3.3.6), and Athanasius set it aside for new believers to read (Festal Letter 39).

outline: Vision 1: Rhoda in heaven accuses Hermas of a sinful thought; the old woman with the book; Hermas must set his household right
Vision 2: the little book copied letter by letter; one repentance before a fixed day; the old woman is the Church, created first of all; copies for Clement and Grapte
Vision 3: the tower built on the waters, its stones, the seven women who hold it up, and the Church growing younger
Vision 4: the great beast on the road, the four colors, and the Church as a bride
Vision 5: the Shepherd, the angel of repentance, comes to live with Hermas
Mandates 1–3: believe in one God; simplicity and giving to all; truth
Mandate 4: purity, an unfaithful wife, divorce and remarriage; the one repentance after baptism
Mandates 5–6: patience and bad temper; the two ways and the two angels
Mandates 10–11: grief and the Holy Spirit; true and false prophets
Mandate 12: evil desire, and whether the commandments can be kept
Similitudes 1–4: the two cities; the elm and the vine; trees in winter and summer
Similitude 5: the true fast; the vineyard and the faithful slave; the flesh in which the Holy Spirit lived
Similitudes 6–7: the shepherds of luxury and of punishment; affliction for Hermas's household
Similitude 8: the willow and the sticks; Michael and the law
Similitude 9.1–15: the twelve mountains of Arcadia, the rock and the gate, the virgins, the building and testing of the tower; the rock and the gate are the Son of God
Similitude 9.16–33: the stones from the deep and the seal; the twelve mountains as twelve kinds of believers; the end of the parable (from 107:3 in Latin)
Similitude 10: the angel's last charge; the virgins left with Hermas

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the Shepherd as a Roman book of the second century: its date (the Muratorian Fragment's brother of Pius, the Clement of 8:3, Harnack's stages), one writer or several, Hermas and Romans 16:14, and how its text survived in two Greek manuscripts, papyri and three ancient versions.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Sets the book beside the New Testament it echoes without quoting: James on double-mindedness and the rich (39; 97), Hebrews 6 on repentance after falling away (6:5; 31), Jesus's teaching on divorce (29), the parables of the vineyard (55), John's gate and way (89), 1 Peter on preaching to the dead (93), and Revelation's visions.

lenses.name: Jewish context
lenses.desc: Hermas's Jewish inheritance: the lost Book of Eldad and Modad, the one writing he names ("Eldad and Modat" in his Greek, 7:4), angels of repentance and of punishment, Michael (69:3), the two angels and the two ways (36), and the form of Jewish apocalypse, each only from texts the notes open.

lenses.name: Doctrine and the churches
lenses.desc: How the churches have read Hermas: repentance after baptism and the history of penance (Tertullian's attack, later Catholic and Orthodox penance, Protestant readings), baptism as the seal (93), the Christology of Similitudes 5 and 9, fasting and the station (54), and the ranks of the Roman church.

lenses.name: Roman world
lenses.desc: The book in its city: slavery (1:1), the Tiber, Cumae and the Sibyl (1:3; 8:1), the Campanian Way (22:2), business, wealth and the household, fasting as a soldier's watch (54:1), Arcadia (78:4), and the elm and vine of Italian farms (51).

sections.b:
The Plain English Translation is made for this site from the Greek and Latin printed by Kirsopp Lake in the Loeb Apostolic Fathers, vol. 2 (1913), as digitized by First1KGreek from its 1917 printing and corrected against the scan of Lake's page. Lake is frank about the text: it "is probably far from good," "neither ℵ nor A is completely trustworthy," and "for so large a part of the book A is the only continuous Greek text." The ancient translations and the quotations in the fathers are, in his words, "too free to be used with confidence." Every place where the Plain English Translation leaves Lake's text, and every reading in his notes that changes the meaning, has a variant entry.

Two ways of numbering. Hermas is usually cited by division: Vision 1–5, Mandate 1–12, Similitude 1–10, each with chapters and sections ("Mandate 4.3.6"). It is also numbered by one series of chapters running through the whole book, 1 to 114. This site uses the running chapters, with Lake's sections as the verses, so Vision 3.8.2 is 16:2, Mandate 4.3.6 is 31:6, and Similitude 9.12.1 is 89:1. Every chapter title begins with the old reference ("Vision 3.8: ..."), so a reader looking for Mandate 4.3 can find it at a glance. Lake's English calls the third division "Parables" (Greek parabolai); the usual name, Similitudes, comes from the Latin similitudines.

The Latin ending. The Athos manuscript ends at 107:2 because its last leaf is lost. From 107:3 to the end Lake prints the old Latin translation, with the few Greek lines that survive set into it (107:3–4 from the Amherst papyrus, 108:5–6 from a quotation in Antiochus, 113:3–5 from Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404). The Plain English Translation follows what Lake prints, Greek where he prints Greek and Latin where he prints Latin, and the chapter pages of 107–114 say so.

sections.h: Sin after baptism and the one repentance
sections.b:
The book's main problem, Lake writes, "is that of sin after baptism." In Hermas's circle "the belief obtained that Christians after baptism were capable of leading sinless lives, and that if they fell they could not again obtain forgiveness." Experience had shown "that in this case few indeed would be saved," and Hermas's message "was that for sin after baptism there was still the possibility of forgiveness for those who repented, though this repentance would not avail more than once." Lake's note at 6:5 calls this "the main point of the 'Shepherd'" and points to Hebrews 6, where it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who have fallen away (Hebrews 6:4–6).

The message comes in two forms. In the Visions the Lord has sworn that sins committed up to a fixed day will be forgiven to those who repent with their whole heart, but not sins after it (6:4–5). In the Mandates the Shepherd says that teachers are right that there is no repentance beyond baptism, yet the Lord in his mercy has given one more repentance to those called before these days; but if anyone sins and repents again and again, it will not help him (31:1–6). Similitudes 6–9 then show how this repentance works, through punishment, cleansing and testing.

Lake sees here "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance." Tertullian, after he became a Montanist, saw the opposite: a book that opened the door to adulterers (see "How the book was read"). Westcott counted the book's teaching on penitence among the proofs of its late date. How the churches read the question of sin after baptism today is on the chapter page of 31 and the cards at Hebrews 6 and Psalm 32.

sections.h: The Church, the tower and the Shepherd
sections.b:
The old woman. In the first visions Hermas meets an old woman in a shining robe who reads to him from a book (2:2; 3:3). He takes her for the Sibyl, the pagan prophetess; a young man tells him she is the Church, old "because she was created the first of all things," and the world was made for her sake (8:1, Lake's translation). In later visions she grows younger and more joyful as her children repent (18–21), and in Vision 4 she appears as a bride (23:1).

The tower. Twice the book shows the Church as a tower being built from stones, once in Vision 3 (10–15) and again, at much greater length, in Similitude 9 (78–110). Square white stones fit at once; others are rejected, cut down or set aside for later. Chapman (1910) notes a change between the two tellings: in Vision 3 "it looked as though only the holy are a part of the Church"; in Similitude 9 "all the baptized are included, though they may be cast out for grave sins, and can be readmitted only after penance." The picture of the church as a building also stands in Ephesians 2:20–22 and 1 Peter 2:5.

The Shepherd. In Vision 5 a glorious man in a shepherd's dress, with a white goatskin, a bag on his shoulders and a staff in his hand, comes to Hermas's house: "the angel of repentance," sent to live with him for the rest of his life (25:1–2, 7). He gives the Mandates and the Similitudes and gives the book its name. Above him stands a glorious angel (66:2), and in Similitude 8 the great and glorious angel is named Michael, who has authority over the people and puts the law into the hearts of believers (69:3). Who these figures are, and how they relate to the Son of God, is set out on the chapter pages of 25, 59, 69 and 89.

sections.h: The Son of God and the Spirit
sections.b:
Hermas never uses the names "Jesus" or "Christ" in Lake's Greek and Latin, except in one reading at 6:8 (see the variant there). He speaks of "the Son of God." In Similitude 5 a faithful slave who tends a vineyard is made his master's heir (55), and the explanation says that God made "the Holy Spirit, which existed before, which created all creation," live in the flesh he chose, and took that flesh as a partner (59:5–7). In Similitude 9 the Shepherd says that the Holy Spirit who spoke to Hermas in the form of the Church "is the Son of God" (78:1), and that the Son is "older than all his creation," the Father's counselor, revealed "in the last days" as the only gate into God's kingdom (89:2–6).

Readers have weighed these words in different ways. Chapman (1910) writes that "it has been thought with some reason that he did not distinguish the Son from the Holy Ghost, or that he held that the Holy Ghost became the Son by His Incarnation," but that "his words are not clear, and his ideas on the subject may have been rather misty and confused than definitely erroneous." Westcott (1896) found the book's teaching on Christ's nature and work "no less harmonious with Apostolic doctrine," with "striking analogies to the Gospel of St John," and judged that Hermas's "peculiar opinions do not degenerate into heresy." The chapter pages of 59 and 89 give the readings in full.

• The Muratorian Fragment, a Latin list of New Testament books, says of the Shepherd: "So it ought indeed to be read, but it cannot be read out publicly to the people in the church, either among the prophets, whose number is complete, or among the apostles, to the end of time" (the site's translation of the Latin in Westcott, 199; the last words, in finem temporum, can also mean the apostles who came "in the end of times," as Chapman takes them). George Reid (1908) reads the fragment as a witness to "the very favourable and perhaps canonical standing enjoyed at Rome by the Apocalypse of Peter and the Shepherd of Hermas." The Fragment's own date and place are disputed (see "Who was Hermas?").
  • Irenaeus (about 180) quotes words found in the first commandment (26:1), on believing first of all in one God who created and completed all things, with the words "well did the Scripture say" (Greek kalōs oun hē graphē hē legousa, kept in Eusebius, Church History 5.8.7; Against Heresies 4.20.2). Eusebius took this to mean that Irenaeus "not only knows, but also receives" the book, and Chapman counts Irenaeus among those who "cite the 'Shepherd' as Scripture." Westcott is more cautious: Irenaeus "does not allude to Hermas by name, nor specify the book from which he derived it," and "it may be reasonably supposed that Hermas here uses words sanctioned by common usage."
  • Clement of Alexandria (about 200) quotes it again and again: the false prophet who speaks some truths (Stromata 1.17; 43), the visions given for the double-minded (1.29), faith and its daughter virtues (2.12), the apostles who went down into the water with those who had died (6.6; 93), and the little book copied letter by letter (6.15; 5:4). Westcott notes that he names Hermas three times but gives him no title of honor.
  • Tertullian (early 200s), writing as a Montanist against a bishop who readmitted adulterers, answered: "I would give way to you if the writing of the Shepherd, the only one that loves adulterers, had deserved to be put into the divine collection, and if it were not judged by every council of the churches, even of yours, among the apocryphal and false writings" (On Modesty 10, the site's translation of the Latin given by Westcott). He adds that the letter he calls Barnabas's, by which he means Hebrews, is "more received among the churches than that apocryphal Shepherd of adulterers" (On Modesty 20). Chapman judges that Tertullian "was no doubt right, that the book had been excluded at Rome from the Bible Instrumentum," but was "exaggerating in referring to 'every council'." He also notes that Tertullian "in his Catholic days" had cited the Shepherd as Scripture, and reads On Modesty 10 as implying that Pope Callistus "had quoted it as an authority (though evidently not as Scripture)."
  • Origen quotes the first commandment from "that little treatise called The Pastor" (On First Principles 1.3.3, a work Rufinus translated into Latin in 397), and in Rufinus's Latin of his Commentary on Romans calls the book "divinely inspired" (above; Prat, 1911). Chapman adds that he "repeatedly apologizes, when he has occasion to quote it, on the ground that 'many people despise it'."
  • Eusebius (about 325) says that some disputed the book, so it could not be placed among the acknowledged books, while others judged it "most necessary," especially for those who needed basic teaching, so that "we know it has already been read publicly in churches" (3.3.6, the site's translation of his Greek). In his list of the New Testament writings he puts "the so-called Shepherd" among the nothoi, the spurious or not genuine books (3.25.4; the NPNF translation has "rejected"), which he still counts among the disputed books, not among the heretics' forgeries (3.25.5–6).
  • Athanasius, in his Festal Letter 39 (367), lists the books of both Testaments and then names others, "not indeed included in the Canon," that the fathers appointed to be read by those newly joining the church: Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd. He himself quotes the first commandment beside Genesis 1:1 from "the most edifying book of the Shepherd" (On the Incarnation 3), cites a saying "as the Shepherd has said" (On the Decrees of Nicaea 4), and when his opponents cited it noted that the book "is not of the Canon" (On the Decrees of Nicaea 18).
  • Jerome (392) writes that the Hermas of Romans 16:14 is said to be the author of the Shepherd, "and it is already read publicly in some churches of Greece. It is in fact a useful book, and many of the old writers drew testimonies from it. But among the Latins it is almost unknown" (Lives of Illustrious Men 10, the site's translation of the Latin). In his preface to Samuel and Kings he puts the Shepherd with Wisdom, Sirach, Judith and Tobit: they "are not in the Canon" (non sunt in Canone; Westcott, 579).
  • Rufinus (about 404) counts "the little book called the Shepherd, or Hermas" among the books the fathers called "ecclesiastical," not canonical: they wished them read in the churches, "but not brought forward to confirm the authority of the faith" (Commentary on the Apostles' Creed 38, from Westcott's Latin, 581). The same clause goes on "which is called the Two Ways or the Judgment of Peter" (qui appellatur Duae viae vel Judicium Petri); the Latin does not make plain whether that names a second book or the Shepherd itself.

sections.h: The witnesses and the Latin ending
sections.b:
Lake lists the witnesses. Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), a Greek Bible "written in the fourth century, probably in Alexandria or the neighbourhood," contains the book from the beginning to Mandate 4.3.6 (1:1–31:6); Chapman says it stands there "with the Epistle of Barnabas at the end of the New Testament," and Lake, introducing Barnabas, says that Barnabas follows "immediately after the Apocalypse, without any suggestion that it belonged to a different category of books" (vol. 1, 338). A, the Athos manuscript of the fifteenth century, once had ten leaves: six are still on Mount Athos, three are at Leipzig, and the last is lost. It was copied by "the celebrated forger Simonides" and later collated by Georgandas, and Lake calls both the copy and the collation "very inaccurate." Chapman's account differs in two details: he calls A "a fourteenth-century manuscript" and says Simonides "stole four of the leaves." A small parchment fragment in Hamburg (H) and papyri from Egypt (Amherst, Oxyrhynchus 404 and 1172, Berlin 5513 and 6789) preserve pieces of the Greek.

There are three ancient translations: two Latin versions, the common one (L1, printed by Faber in Paris in 1513) and the Palatine (L2), an Ethiopic version (E) found by d'Abbadie, and fragments of a Coptic version in the Sahidic dialect (C). Clement of Alexandria, a writer Lake calls pseudo-Athanasius, and Antiochus of Palestine quote it. Chapman notes that the book "went out of fashion in the East, so that the Greek manuscripts of it are but two in number, whereas in the West it became better known and was frequently copied in the Middle Ages."

Because A has lost its last leaf, the Greek breaks off at 107:2 (Similitude 9.30.2). From there to the end the book is known from the Latin, with a few Greek lines from the Amherst papyrus (107:3–4), a quotation in Antiochus (108:5–6) and Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 404 (113:3–5). The notes on those chapters give the Latin wherever the sense turns on it.

Hermas quotes almost nothing in so many words. The one writing he names is "Eldad and Modat": "as it is written in Eldad and Modat, who prophesied to the people in the wilderness" (7:4; the Greek has no word for "book"). In English the lost work is usually called the Book of Eldad and Modad, after the two men who prophesied in the camp in Numbers 11:26 (Eldad and Medad). From it he takes the saying that the Lord is near to those who turn back. Chapman calls it the "one direct quotation" in the book and says "the reference is apparently ironical." Chapman adds that "there are many indirect citations from the Old Testament," that Hermas shows knowledge of the Gospels, and that "the books he most certainly and most often uses are the Epistle of St. James and the Apocalypse." Lake's margin points again and again to James: at double-mindedness in 39:6 he cites James 1:8. It points to the Gospels: at divorce in 29:6 to Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:11, and at the rich and the kingdom in 97:2 to Matthew 19:23. It points to John: at the gate and the way in 89:3–6 to John 3:5 and John 14:6. And it points to Ephesians: at one body and one Spirit in 90:5–7 to Ephesians 4:4. The notes give each echo where it occurs.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Shepherd comes to live with Hermas as in Psalm 23
spec.body: The Shepherd's first words are that he has been sent "to live with you the rest of the days of your life" (25:2; Greek hina meta sou oikēsō tas loipas hēmeras tēs zōēs sou). The Greek Psalm 23 (22 in the Septuagint), which begins with the LORD as shepherd (Psalm 23:1), ends with mercy following the speaker "all the days of my life" and his dwelling in the house of the Lord (Greek pasas tas hēmeras tēs zōēs mou, kai to katoikein me en oikō Kyriou; Psalm 23:6). The book's title figure, a shepherd who comes to dwell with a man for the days of his life, may be meant to recall that psalm, so that the angel of repentance acts out the Lord's shepherding in a Roman house. Lake's margin gives no reference to Psalm 23 here, and the shared words are common ones; the link is mine.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Church takes the Sibyl's place
spec.body: Hermas first meets the old woman with the book on the road to Cumae (1:3; 5:1, if the editors' Cumae is right), and his first guess is that she is the Sibyl (8:1), the pagan prophetess. Virgil had already set the Sibyl's cave at Cumae and called her "the Cumaean Sibyl" (Cumaea Sibylla, Aeneid 6.2, 10, 98). The young man corrects him: she is the Church, older than the world. The setting may be chosen to make a point to Roman readers: the book of revelation they should listen to is not the Sibyl's, but the Church's, and she, not the Sibyl, is the oldest of all. Lake notes the editors' Cumae, the Latin's "city of Ostia" and the alternative reading of a trip to the country, and does not draw this link; it is mine, and it depends on the reading Cumae.

prompts: The old woman on the white chair (Vision 1)

A tired middle-aged Roman man in a plain tunic kneels in a rough field above a river gorge; in front of him a large white chair made of snowy wool, and on it an elderly woman in a shining robe reads aloud from a scroll held open in both hands; in the far distance a road winding toward a seaside town. Style: sketched by hand onto an old parchment scroll in sepia and iron-gall ink with charcoal shading, washes of red and yellow ochre like cave paintings, small Greek letters along the margin, a few bold flat shapes of deep blue like modern paper cut-outs; soft, torn edges fading into the parchment, never a hard rectangle.
The tower built on the waters (Vision 3)

Six young men in white directing many workers who carry square white stones up from the depths of a lake and from the land, fitting them into a great round tower rising from the water; other stones, cracked, rough or round, lie rejected around its foot; an old woman on an ivory couch watches with Hermas beside her. Style: hand-drawn on a parchment scroll in ink and charcoal, with stones colored in soft ochre and chalk white, a few stick-figure workers in the manner of cave drawings, flat modern-art blocks of blue for the water; soft edges blending into the scroll.

A Roman man sits on a bed in a small room after praying; through the door comes a tall, glorious man dressed as a shepherd, a white goatskin over his shoulders, a leather bag on his back and a staff in his hand, raising his hand in greeting; an oil lamp lights the wall. Style: sketched onto an ancient scroll in sepia ink with charcoal, red-ochre pigment, faint Greek letters, and one flat shape of deep blue for the night outside; torn, faded edges, never a hard rectangle.

Twelve mountains of different colors and shapes in a ring around a wide plain; in the middle a great square white rock, older than the mountains, with a newly cut gate shining like the sun; twelve virgins in linen stand at the gate as stones are carried through it. Style: hand-drawn on a parchment scroll in ink and soft watercolor, mountains drawn like cave paintings in ochre, black and green, the gate in bright gold leaf with a flat modern-art glow; soft edges, no frame.

The older public-domain English translation, offered beside the Plain English Translation for checking.
B. F. Westcott, A General Survey of the History of the Canon of the New Testament (1896)
Pages 199–207 weigh the Muratorian Fragment, Origen and Tertullian on the Shepherd, and Hermas's teaching on faith and on Christ.
A Catholic survey of the book's contents, its date and authorship, the theories of several authors, and its manuscripts and versions.

canon.summary: The Shepherd of Hermas is a Christian book of visions, commandments and parables written in Rome in the second century. None of the churches whose canon is set out below has it in its Bible. In the early church it stood at the edge of the canon: Eusebius read Irenaeus as receiving it as Scripture, Origen called it "divinely inspired" (in Rufinus's Latin), Codex Sinaiticus copied it after the New Testament, and some churches read it in public. But the Muratorian Fragment, Eusebius, Athanasius and Jerome set it outside the canon: the Fragment and Athanasius still recommended it for reading, Jerome called it "a useful book," and Eusebius put it among the spurious books.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of the New Testament books (1546) does not include it; that decree is the one church document in this row. George Reid, writing in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), traces the decision at Rome back to the Roman synod of 382 under Pope Damasus, whose list, he says, is preserved in the Decretum Gelasianum, "a compilation partly of the sixth century, but containing much material dating from the two preceding ones"; with that synod, in Reid's account, "the Shepherd and the false Apocalypse of Peter now received their final blow." John Chapman, in the same encyclopedia (1910), calls it "a work which had great authority in ancient times and was ranked with Holy Scripture," and sees in it the Roman church of the second century.

Not in the New Testament as Reid (1908) describes it: the Eastern Orthodox churches "have a New Testament identical with the Catholic." The Council in Trullo (692) confirmed the canons of the Council of Laodicea and of Athanasius among others (canon 2). Laodicea forbids reading "uncanonical books" in church (canon 59), and its list of the New Testament books, whose genuineness its English editor calls "most questionable," does not include the Shepherd (canon 60), though it leaves out Revelation too, so its silence settles little; Athanasius sets the Shepherd outside the canon, among the books for new believers (Festal Letter 39). This page found no present-day Orthodox statement that names the Shepherd. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates the Apostle Hermas of the Seventy on May 31 as a bishop of Philippopolis, and says that "according to Tradition, Saint Hermas is the author of The Shepherd, an instructive book based on revelations from angels."

Not in its Bible. The church's list of its 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books of church order to the 27, does not include the Shepherd. An Ethiopic translation of the book does exist (Lake's witness E).

Not among the books George Reid, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), says these churches add to the New Testament: "The Armenians have one apocryphal letter to the Corinthians and two from the same. The Coptic-Arabic Church include with the canonical Scriptures the Apostolic Constitutions and the Clementine Epistles." This page found no present-day statement of the Coptic or Armenian churches that names the Shepherd. Fragments of a Coptic translation in the Sahidic dialect survive (Lake's witness C).

Not Scripture. Article VI receives "All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received"; the Shepherd is not one of them, nor among the "other Books" the Church reads for example of life.

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament, "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life" (1.2). Its words on "the books commonly called Apocrypha" (1.3) concern the deuterocanon, not early Christian writings; the Shepherd is simply not in its list.
Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 New Testament books (1.2); the Shepherd is not among them.

provenance.b: The book was written in Greek in Rome by a Christian named Hermas, who says that the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda (1:1) and who sets his visions on the roads around the city (1:2–3; 22:2). The Muratorian Fragment says he wrote it "very recently, in our own times," while his brother Pius was bishop of Rome (the Fragment's own date is disputed: see "Who was Hermas?"); Lake puts Pius "about 148 A.D." and adds that "many critics" think the book was written in stages over the twenty or thirty years before. The book says it was written down in stages (8:2–3; 25:5–7; 78:1).

It was read far from Rome. Irenaeus in Gaul quoted words from it about 180, Clement of Alexandria and Origen used it often, and the Muratorian Fragment argued about where it belonged. Eusebius knew churches that read it publicly (3.3.6), and Jerome knew some in Greece that still did (10). It was translated into Latin, Ethiopic and Coptic. Codex Sinaiticus copies it after the New Testament and the Epistle of Barnabas (Chapman; Lake, vol. 1, 338, on Barnabas following Revelation there). Chapman notes that it later "went out of fashion in the East," while in the West it "was frequently copied in the Middle Ages" in Latin.

The Latin was printed first, by Faber in Paris in 1513 (Lake). The Greek became known only in the nineteenth century, from the Athos manuscript, which the forger Simonides copied (Lake; Chapman adds that he also sold a Greek text he had composed himself, published in 1856 before the fraud was found out), and from Codex Sinaiticus, published by Tischendorf in 1862 (Chapman). Papyri from Egypt have since added pieces of the Greek, including some of the lost ending (Lake).

• Jewish apocalypse and the lost Book of Eldad and Modad ("Eldad and Modat" in Hermas's Greek), the one writing it names (7:4), in a reference Chapman calls "apparently ironical."
  • The letter of James, on double-mindedness, the rich and the poor, and resisting the devil (Lake's margin at 39:6, 45:4, 97:2; Chapman).
  • The Gospels, above all Jesus's sayings on divorce (29:6) and on the rich (97:2), and John's gate and way (89:3–6).
  • Paul's letters, above all Ephesians (90:5–7; 94:4).
  • Revelation, the other great Christian apocalypse, which Chapman counts with James among the books Hermas "most certainly and most often uses."

rejected_why.b: The Muratorian Fragment gives the reason in one line: it was written "very recently, in our own times," so it cannot be placed among the prophets, "whose number is complete," or among the apostles. A book by the brother of a second-century bishop could not carry an apostle's authority. Westcott (1896), who accepted the fragment's date, held that "evidence however both internal and external is decisive against a belief in its Apostolic date." The case for an older date rested on Origen's guess that the writer was the Hermas of Romans 16:14, which Westcott calls "nothing more than a conjecture." The argument from date is only as strong as the Fragment's witness: Chapman thinks its statement that Hermas wrote while Pius was bishop "may similarly be an inference" from a list of popes, and the Fragment's own date is disputed (see "Who was Hermas?").

Tertullian rejected it for what it taught: "the only one that loves adulterers" (On Modesty 10), "that apocryphal Shepherd of adulterers" (On Modesty 20). He wrote as a Montanist against the readmission of serious sinners, and Chapman judges that he was "exaggerating" when he claimed every council had rejected it, "for the teaching of the 'Pastor' was in direct contradiction with his own rigid views as to penance." Westcott notes that Tertullian's words show the question of the canon was being argued in Christian assemblies in his day.

rejected_why.h: Disputed, then set aside for reading
rejected_why.b: Eusebius saw that some churches valued it and some disputed it, and he placed it among the spurious books (3.3.6; 3.25.4). Athanasius kept it for new believers but not in the canon (Festal Letter 39), and Rufinus put it among the "ecclesiastical" books read in church "but not brought forward to confirm the authority of the faith." In the West, Jerome found it "almost unknown" among the Latins and listed it among the books that "are not in the Canon." The Latin list of Codex Claromontanus still names it, after the Acts of the Apostles, but a later hand marked it and three other books there with a dash (Westcott, 574–576).

cited_in.b: Paul greets a Hermas among the Christians in Rome. Origen, in Rufinus's Latin, guessed that he was the writer of the Shepherd, and Jerome and the Orthodox Church in America repeat the tradition; the Muratorian Fragment makes the writer a brother of Pius, bishop about 148 (Lake), and Westcott calls the identification "nothing more than a conjecture." Even if it were right, Romans says nothing of the book.

Hebrews says it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who have fallen away. Lake's note at 6:5 sets the Shepherd's one repentance against this "primitive teaching": Hermas "now states that it has been revealed to him" that sin will be forgiven to those who repent up to a fixed day. Tertullian used Hebrews against the Shepherd (On Modesty 20). Whether Hermas knew Hebrews, or both reflect the same early teaching, the book does not say.

James's double-minded man, unsteady in all his ways, is the theme of the ninth commandment and of the whole book, which uses "double-minded" and "double-mindedness" again and again (39). Lake's margin points to James 1:8, and Chapman counts James among the books Hermas uses most. The Shepherd uses James, not the other way around.

Jesus's saying that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery lies behind Mandate 4, where a husband must send away a wife who will not stop committing adultery, but may not marry another, so that she can repent and return (29:4–8). Lake's margin points to Mark 10:11, Matthew 5:32, Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:11.

1 Peter says Christ preached to the spirits in prison (1 Peter 3:19; compare 1 Peter 4:6). Similitude 9 goes further: the apostles and teachers, after their own deaths, preached to those who had died before and gave them the seal of baptism (93:5–7). Clement of Alexandria already quotes the passage (Stromata 6.6). The Shepherd builds on the early Christian belief; it is not a source for 1 Peter.

Ephesians pictures the church as a building on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple (compare 1 Peter 2:5, living stones). The Shepherd turns the picture into its two long visions of the tower built from stones (10–15; 78–110), in which the rock and the gate are the Son of God (89:1–6).

Eldad and Medad, who prophesied in the camp, give their names to the lost Book of Eldad and Modad, which the Shepherd quotes as written ("in Eldad and Modat," 7:4). Numbers does not mention a book; the link is through the later work named for them.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how Christians in Rome lived, prayed, sinned and repented in the second century, the Shepherd is a rich source: long, personal, full of daily life, and widely read. Its text is insecure, by Lake's own judgment: the Greek rests for most of the book on one late and badly copied manuscript, and the ending survives only in Latin. Its visions make no claim that can be checked as history, and its own historical details (Clement, Grapte, Maximus) are few and debated. Measured against the 66 books it agrees with them on much, goes beyond them in its pictures and in its one repentance with a fixed day, and in its language about the Son and the Spirit is unclear enough that Christians have read it both as orthodox and as confused.

sections.h: 1. A witness to the Roman church: very high
sections.b: The book shows a church of house congregations with elders who lead, overseers who shelter the needy and widows (104:2), teachers, deacons and prophets, true and false (13:1; 43). It shows Christians in business and trade, rich and poor (14; 51; 97), denial and trial before the authorities (6:8; 14:5; 74:4; 105:4), fasting and almsgiving (54–56), and above all the pastoral crisis of what to do with baptized believers who fall. It was read, quoted and argued over across the church for two centuries (Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Jerome).

Lake judges the text "probably far from good." Codex Sinaiticus is old but covers only the first quarter (to 31:6). For most of the rest the only continuous Greek is A, a fifteenth-century manuscript copied by a forger and collated hastily, and it has lost its last leaf, so the end (107:3–114:5) rests on the Latin with a few Greek lines. Papyri from Egypt check A here and there and show, Lake says, that neither ℵ nor A "is completely trustworthy." The Latin, Ethiopic and Coptic versions help, but Lake finds them "too free to be used with confidence." The general sense of the book is secure; individual words often are not, and the variant entries say where.

The visions are presented as experiences, and nothing in them can be checked as history. The book's few historical details raise questions rather than settle them: the Clement of 8:3 points to the 90s, the Muratorian Fragment to the 140s, and Origen's identification with the Hermas of Romans 16:14 to an even earlier writer. Chapman thinks the most probable view is that the historical details are a literary device and that the writer was the brother of Pius; Lake leaves open whether the book was written over twenty or thirty years. The setting in Rome is secure.

• Matches: one God who created all things from nothing (26:1, as Hebrews 11:3); repentance and forgiveness for those who turn back; faith and the virtues as the Church's support (16); care for widows and orphans (27; 50:8, as James 1:27); the danger of riches (14:5–7; 97:2, as Matthew 19:23); the church as a building of living stones (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Peter 2:5); the Son of God as the only way to the Father (89:6, as John 14:6).
  • Goes beyond: a single repentance after baptism with a fixed day (6:4–5; 31:6), which goes past anything the New Testament says (the closest is Hebrews 6:4–6, which reads the other way); the apostles preaching to and baptizing the dead (93:5, beyond 1 Peter 3:19); extra merit for good done beyond the commandments (56:3); angels with names and tasks (Thegri over the beasts at 23:4; the angel of punishment at 66:2).
  • Tension or conflict: the language that makes the Holy Spirit "the Son of God" (78:1) and the flesh in which the Spirit lived God's "partner" (59:5–7) is, on Chapman's reading, at least unclear and on one reading conflicts with the New Testament's teaching that the Word, the Son, became flesh (John 1:14); Westcott reads the same passages as in harmony with apostolic doctrine. The chapter pages of 59 and 89 give both sides. A rule that a husband must not remarry after sending away an unfaithful wife (29:8) is stricter than some readings of Matthew 19:9 and matches others; the site's cards on divorce give the churches' answers.

how_to_read.b: None of the churches whose canon is set out above has the Shepherd in its Bible. Read it as Athanasius and Rufinus advised: a book for learning the Christian life, "not brought forward to confirm the authority of the faith." It is a window into a Roman congregation a century after Paul wrote to Rome.
The old woman, the tower, the beast and the twelve mountains are explained in the book itself. Read the explanation with each vision, and do not press the details further than Hermas does.

Its one repentance was a pastoral offer to a church that thought fallen Christians had no hope. Ask what it meant to them before using it to settle later questions about penance or the forgiveness of serious sin, and read it beside Hebrews 6, 1 John 1:9 and the cards at Hebrews 6 and Psalm 32.

how_to_read.h: Weigh its words about the Son
how_to_read.b: Where Hermas speaks of the Son and the Spirit (59; 78:1; 89), read the notes and the views on those pages. Rufinus, who wanted it read in the churches, said it was not to be "brought forward to confirm the authority of the faith."
